none_fit.heading: This test does not apply to U.S. citizens or green card holders
none_fit.result_copy: The Substantial Presence Test decides whether a non-citizen is treated as a U.S. resident for tax purposes. If you are a U.S. citizen or a lawful permanent resident (green card holder), it does not apply to you — but not because you are outside the U.S. tax net. Citizens and green card holders are taxed on worldwide income regardless of how many days they spend in the United States, and regardless of where they live. A day count will not change that. If you are trying to reduce or exit that obligation, the question is expatriation or treaty relief, not day counting, and it is worth a conversation with a qualified U.S. tax professional.

insufficient_information.heading: Your position needs a closer look
insufficient_information.result_copy: Your answers do not yet establish your U.S. tax residency position — either whether this test applies to you at all, or how many days you were physically present in the current year. Both matter: the Substantial Presence Test requires at least 31 days of presence in the current year AND a weighted three-year total of at least 183 days, counting all days in the current year, one third of the days in the year before, and one sixth of the days in the year before that. Some days may not count at all — days in transit through the U.S. under 24 hours, days as a crew member of a foreign vessel, regular commuting days from Canada or Mexico, days you could not leave because of a medical condition, and days as an exempt individual. Establishing your day count is the first step, and a short personalised review sets it out.
